items.question: What does it mean for a claim in model output to be grounded?

options.A: The claim is supported by the model's high-confidence parametric memory
options.B: The claim traces back to material actually present in the context window
options.C: The claim has been independently verified by a human reviewer
options.D: The claim uses hedging language that signals the model's uncertainty

items.question: What distinguishes a knowledge-cutoff staleness error from a hallucination?

options.A: Staleness produces grammatically unusual text; hallucination produces fluent text
options.B: Staleness is limited to numerical data; hallucination can affect any claim type
options.C: Staleness can always be corrected by improving the prompt; hallucination requires a newer model
options.D: Staleness describes a fact that was accurate at training time but is now outdated; hallucination describes a claim that was never accurate

items.question: Among the following, which claim type carries the highest fabrication risk in model output?

options.A: A general description of how a common business process typically works
options.B: A named study or report paired with a specific year and a precise statistic
options.C: A paraphrase of a concept the model was asked to explain
options.D: A bullet-point list of generic recommendations without attributions

items.question: What is parametric memory in the context of language model outputs?

options.A: Knowledge encoded in the model's weights during training, not retrieved from context at inference time
options.B: A session-level memory that stores the last several turns of a conversation
options.C: A retrieval mechanism that fetches relevant documents from a knowledge base at query time
options.D: A cached version of the system prompt reused across multiple sessions

items.question: What term describes a citation in model output that names a plausible-sounding but nonexistent source?

options.A: Conflation
options.B: Fabricated citation
options.C: Paraphrase error
options.D: Attribution gap

items.question: Which failure mode describes model output citing a fact that was true at training time but has since changed?

options.A: Staleness, because the model reproduced accurate-at-training knowledge that is now outdated
options.B: Hallucination, because the cited fact is no longer correct
options.C: Omission, because the model failed to mention the change
options.D: Commission error, because the model introduced a claim that is factually incorrect

items.question: Which TWO claim types are generally considered highest risk for fabrication and therefore require source verification before any external use? (Choose TWO)

options.A: General summaries of how a well-known industry process typically works
options.B: Direct quotations attributed to a named individual
options.C: High-level descriptions of a product category with no specific figures
options.D: Specific statistics attributed to a named research publication
options.E: Paraphrases of concepts the model was asked to define

items.question: Which characteristic of model output is the most reliable signal that source verification is needed?

options.A: The response is significantly longer than previous responses to similar prompts
options.B: The model used hedging language somewhere in the response
options.C: The prompt did not specify a citation format requirement
options.D: The output contains specific, attributable claims such as statistics, named sources, or publication titles

items.question: Grounding is a statement about provenance, not about truth. Which implication follows directly from this distinction?

options.A: A grounded claim is always factually correct because it originated from a real source in context
options.B: An ungrounded claim is always a fabrication and should be treated as false
options.C: Grounding guarantees that a claim will survive independent fact-checking by a human reviewer
options.D: A grounded claim can still be factually wrong if the source document it traces to contains an error

items.question: What is the primary purpose of sampling model output rather than reviewing every item in a bulk task?

options.A: Sampling is required by data protection law before model output can be shared externally
options.B: Sampling provides a cost-effective estimate of overall output quality and can surface systematic errors without exhaustive review
options.C: Checking every item is computationally impossible for language models processing large volumes
options.D: Sampling allows the reviewer to skip items that appear grammatically correct

items.question: What is the difference between an omission error and a commission error in model output?

options.A: An omission error is always less serious than a commission error because nothing false is stated
options.B: Omission errors appear in summaries; commission errors appear in extractions
options.C: An omission error occurs when required information is absent from the output; a commission error occurs when incorrect information is actively stated
options.D: An omission error results from too short a context window; a commission error results from context window overflow

items.question: Which TWO practices characterize a well-designed verification workflow for high-volume model output? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Reviewing only items where the model explicitly expressed low confidence or used hedging language
options.B: Accepting all items that pass an automated spell-check without further human review
options.C: Cross-referencing a random sample of outputs against the source documents used as input
options.D: Asking the model to critique its own output to replace the need for human review
options.E: Documenting that verification occurred, including who performed it and when

items.question: When verifying a model-generated summary, which failure mode should the reviewer prioritise checking?

options.A: Whether the summary omits material facts that are present in the source document
options.B: Whether the summary uses the citation format specified in the style guide
options.C: Whether the summary is shorter than the original document
options.D: Whether the summary uses first-person or third-person voice consistently

items.question: What is the purpose of cross-referencing model output against a system of record?

options.A: To improve the model's response speed on subsequent queries in the same session
options.B: To confirm the model used the correct output format as specified in the prompt
options.C: To ensure the model's claims about current state align with authoritative data the model did not generate
options.D: To identify which portions of the output originated from parametric memory rather than context

items.question: Which TWO conditions together justify exhaustive review of all model output rather than sampling? (Choose TWO)

options.A: The output will directly influence a consequential decision with no further human review step
options.B: The model was given a well-structured prompt with several worked examples
options.C: The output domain is one where the model typically performs well
options.D: Individual errors in the output cannot be corrected once the output has been acted upon
options.E: The output will be circulated only as an internal working draft

items.question: What is the primary function of documentation in a model-output verification workflow?

options.A: Documentation enables the model to recall which outputs were already verified in previous sessions
options.B: Documentation is required only when output will be shared with parties external to the organisation
options.C: Documentation creates an audit trail establishing that human review occurred and who is accountable for the verified output
options.D: Documentation improves the quality of the model's next response by recording what errors were found

items.question: When verifying a model-generated extraction, what class of error should the reviewer specifically check for beyond factual accuracy?

options.A: Whether the model explained its extraction criteria for each item selected
options.B: Whether the extracted items use the same typographic formatting as the source document
options.C: Omissions: important items present in the source that the model failed to extract
options.D: Whether the total count of extracted items matches a number specified in the prompt

items.question: Which TWO statements correctly describe the relationship between spot-checking and systematic verification? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Spot-checking is a complete substitute for systematic verification when the output volume is too high for full review
options.B: Spot-checking a random sample can surface recurring error patterns without reviewing every item
options.C: Systematic verification is only warranted after spot-checks have already found errors
options.D: A random spot-check sample can provide reasonable confidence about overall output quality while remaining cost-effective
options.E: Spot-checking is appropriate only for extractive tasks; generative tasks require exhaustive review

items.question: A reviewer confirms all extracted values match the source document. Which risk does this check NOT address?

options.A: The extracted values may have formatting inconsistencies relative to the source
options.B: The model may have produced an unrelated fabricated citation elsewhere in the same output
options.C: The source document itself may contain an error that the model accurately reproduced
options.D: The extraction may be missing fields that appear in the source but were not extracted

items.question: What does 'calibration' mean as a property of model output confidence?

options.A: A well-calibrated model expresses high confidence when it is likely correct and appropriate uncertainty when it may be wrong
options.B: A calibrated model always produces factually accurate outputs regardless of the topic
options.C: Calibration is the process of grounding claims in source documents before generating output
options.D: A calibrated model never uses hedging language on topics within its training domain

items.question: What is the key distinction between grounding and calibration as properties of model output?

options.A: Grounding applies to factual claims only; calibration applies to opinion and recommendation statements
options.B: Grounding is about where a claim comes from; calibration is about whether the model's expressed confidence matches its actual reliability
options.C: Grounding is a technical property detectable by automated tools; calibration requires human judgment to assess
options.D: Grounding improves with more training data; calibration improves primarily with model size

items.question: A model produces an ungrounded claim that a subsequent fact-check confirms is accurate. What remains true about that claim at the time it was used?

options.A: The claim becomes retroactively grounded once its accuracy is independently confirmed
options.B: The claim required no verification because the correct result justifies the process
options.C: The claim was still unverified at the point of use, regardless of its eventual accuracy
options.D: The accurate parametric recall demonstrates the model's calibration is reliable for this topic

items.question: What is the defining characteristic of 'plausible-but-false' detail in model output?

options.A: The output contains errors throughout, not concentrated in one area
options.B: The false detail is structurally inconsistent with surrounding content and can be identified by careful reading
options.C: The false detail is detectable by grammar and spell-check tools
options.D: The false detail is indistinguishable from accurate output by surface inspection and requires source verification to detect

items.question: Which type of model output generally does NOT require source verification before use?

options.A: A brainstorm list of potential options or ideas with no specific attributed claims
options.B: A summary of a document the model was given as context
options.C: A response citing industry statistics the model recalls from its training
options.D: A paraphrase of a specific regulation the model was asked to explain

items.question: Verification and evaluation are both output quality practices. What is their primary distinction?

options.A: Verification is performed by humans; evaluation is performed by automated scoring tools
options.B: Verification checks whether a specific output is correct against a known reference; evaluation assesses output quality against defined criteria across a sample or population of outputs
options.C: Verification applies to factual claims; evaluation applies to stylistic and tonal quality
options.D: Verification is performed before output is used; evaluation is performed after errors are reported by end users

items.question: What is the primary limitation of using the model's expressed confidence as the main trigger for deciding whether to verify output?

options.A: Expressed confidence is encoded in metadata the reviewer cannot easily read
options.B: High-confidence outputs are always longer and take more time to review than low-confidence ones
options.C: A model can express high confidence about a fabricated claim and hedge on a true one — confidence is a property of generation style, not of factual accuracy
options.D: Using confidence as a proxy reduces review time but substantially increases the cost per check

items.question: For a claim to be both grounded and accurate, which TWO conditions must both be satisfied? (Choose TWO)

options.A: The claim traces to a source actually present in the context window at generation time
options.B: The claim uses hedging language to reflect the model's uncertainty about the source
options.C: The source the claim traces to is itself factually correct about the matter being claimed
options.D: The claim was reviewed and confirmed by a human reviewer before use
options.E: The claim is stated in the same words as the source with no paraphrase

items.question: When is it most important that verification be performed by someone other than the person who authored the original prompt?

options.A: When the output is longer than a single page and requires extended reading time
options.B: When the model was given a poorly structured prompt with no examples
options.C: When the task involved uploading a document to the context window
options.D: When the verification result will be used to establish accountability for a consequential decision

items.question: What does spot-checking model output mean in a verification context?

options.A: Reviewing a small, targeted subset of items to assess quality without exhaustive review of every item
options.B: Running automated grammar and spell-check tools across the complete output
options.C: Asking the model to regenerate its response to see whether the results are consistent across runs
options.D: Comparing only the first and last items in a batch to detect any drift across the batch

items.question: In a summary drawn from multiple source documents, which omission type poses the highest substantive risk?

options.A: Omitting the title or author metadata of the source documents from the summary header
options.B: Omitting a finding from one source that contradicts or qualifies a claim made using another source
options.C: Omitting documents that were in context but happened not to be referenced by the model
options.D: Omitting the date on which the summary was generated

items.question: Which scenario best illustrates that grounding and accuracy are orthogonal — independently variable — properties?

options.A: A model produces a fabricated citation with no source in context, and the citation is inaccurate
options.B: A model accurately summarises a document that was provided in the context window
options.C: A model accurately reproduces a factual error that was present in the source document provided in the context window
options.D: A model produces an ungrounded claim that cannot be checked because no source was provided

items.question: What is the primary purpose of defining a sampling rate before verifying bulk model output?

options.A: A pre-defined sampling rate ensures the reviewer always starts with the most important items in the batch
options.B: Sampling rates are mandated by most data governance frameworks before AI output can be shared externally
options.C: Sampling rates determine how long the model should take to generate each item in the batch
options.D: Pre-defining a sampling rate makes the review plan explicit and defensible, ensuring scope is proportionate to stakes before the review begins

items.question: Why is 'plausible-but-false' detail especially dangerous in model output relative to obviously incorrect output?

options.A: It passes surface-level reading because it is stylistically and contextually consistent with surrounding accurate content
options.B: It is produced only when the model is given a poorly constructed prompt without worked examples
options.C: It always takes the form of a hallucination rather than a staleness error, making it harder to categorise
options.D: It is systematically more common in short outputs than in long ones

items.question: Which factor most directly determines whether model output should be reviewed exhaustively rather than by sampling?

options.A: The model tier used to generate the output
options.B: Whether individual errors in the output can be corrected after the output has been acted upon
options.C: The length of the output measured in words or tokens
options.D: Whether the output was generated from a well-structured, tested prompt

items.question: Which TWO observations suggest a verification workflow is insufficient even if initial review finds no errors? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Reviewers are checking each output against the source for commission errors but never running the source-to-output direction to check for omissions
options.B: The model consistently uses hedging language across most of its responses
options.C: Verification is performed but no record is kept of who reviewed which items or when
options.D: The model is run at a tier lower than the maximum available for the task type
options.E: The same prompt template is reused across all items in the batch without per-item customization

items.question: Why is a direct quotation attributed to a named individual considered especially high-risk for fabrication in model output?

options.A: Named individuals are not mentioned in training data, so the model has no basis for producing quotes attributed to them
options.B: Direct quotations require a citation format the model cannot reliably produce
options.C: The claim asserts a specific person said specific words — a highly specific, verifiable, and reputation-affecting assertion the model can fabricate convincingly
options.D: Quotation marks signal to reviewers that the content is speculative and should not be relied upon

items.question: Which TWO conditions must both be met for cross-referencing model output against a document to constitute valid verification? (Choose TWO)

options.A: The reviewer has access to the original source document, not only the model's summary or extract of it
options.B: The model was given the source document as context rather than producing claims from parametric memory
options.C: The cross-reference covers both commission errors and omission errors — checking in both directions
options.D: The cross-reference is completed within a specified time window after the model generates the output
options.E: The cross-reference is conducted by a credentialed subject-matter expert rather than a generalist reviewer

items.question: At what point in a workflow should verification of model output occur relative to external use of that output?

options.A: Verification can be completed after external use if the output was generated by a reliable model tier
options.B: Verification should occur during output generation by configuring the model to check its own work
options.C: Verification is most efficiently performed reactively once end users report specific errors
options.D: Verification must be completed before the output is shared externally or acted upon

items.question: Which TWO properties of a source document directly affect the reliability of grounded claims derived from it? (Choose TWO)

options.A: The length of the source document in pages or words
options.B: Whether the source document is current relative to the claims being made from it
options.C: The file format in which the source document was uploaded to the context
options.D: Whether the source document itself originates from an authoritative and accurate origin
options.E: Whether the source document was uploaded by the user or retrieved through a connector

items.question: What does it mean for a model's output to be well-calibrated?

options.A: The output contains no factual errors.
options.B: The model's expressed certainty aligns with the actual probability that its claims are correct.
options.C: Every uncertain claim is accompanied by explicit hedging language.
options.D: The model declines to answer questions it cannot independently verify.

items.question: What behavior is described as sycophancy in a language model?

options.A: Generating fluent but factually incorrect responses to avoid refusing a request.
options.B: Producing inconsistent answers across repeated runs of the same prompt.
options.C: Adjusting responses to reflect what the user appears to want to hear rather than what is accurate or genuinely helpful.
options.D: Defaulting to excessive hedging language on every claim to avoid appearing overconfident.

items.question: In output evaluation, what is a golden set?

options.A: A curated collection of reference outputs representing correct or high-quality responses for known inputs.
options.B: A set of prompts that reliably produce consistent outputs across repeated runs.
options.C: The highest-scoring outputs from a benchmarking run, retained for future comparison.
options.D: A list of approved phrasings stored in project instructions to enforce style consistency.

items.question: Which category of output error is exemplified when Claude calculates 15% of 240 as 42?

options.A: Calibration failure, because the model expressed confidence in an uncertain computation.
options.B: Internal inconsistency, because the result contradicts the model's own stated method.
options.C: Hallucination, because the figure was generated from parametric memory rather than retrieved.
options.D: Arithmetic error, because the computed value is mathematically wrong regardless of confidence or grounding.

items.question: What is the intended function of hedging phrases such as 'this may vary' or 'I am not certain' in Claude's output?

options.A: To reduce output length by substituting brief qualifications for detailed justification.
options.B: To signal to the reader that a claim carries uncertainty and warrants independent verification.
options.C: To transfer liability for incorrect statements from the model to the user.
options.D: To indicate that the claim is grounded in retrieved material rather than parametric memory.

items.question: Which best describes an internal logical inconsistency in a Claude output?

options.A: A claim that contradicts an externally verified fact.
options.B: A conclusion reached without citing supporting evidence.
options.C: Two statements within the same output that cannot simultaneously be true.
options.D: A response that fails to address all parts of the original question.

items.question: What is the primary purpose of asking Claude to critique its own output?

options.A: To surface errors, contradictions, or gaps that Claude can correct before the output is used.
options.B: To confirm that the output is grounded in the documents supplied in the context window.
options.C: To reduce the token cost of subsequent refinement turns by catching problems early.
options.D: To trigger extended reasoning for deeper analysis of the same task.

items.question: A response states a contested empirical claim as settled fact without qualification. What type of output problem does this represent?

options.A: Hallucination, because the claim was not retrieved from a grounded source.
options.B: Simultaneous calibration failure and hallucination, since the two always co-occur.
options.C: Sycophancy, because the model reflected confident framing from the user's prompt.
options.D: Overconfident tone, because the claim is presented with more certainty than the evidence warrants.

items.question: What is the primary function of an evaluation rubric in output review?

options.A: To define which outputs are acceptable and which must be rejected.
options.B: To enumerate the factual claims that require independent verification.
options.C: To provide scored dimensions against which output quality is measured consistently.
options.D: To specify the format and structure the output must follow.

items.question: Why should acceptance criteria be defined before output is generated rather than after?

options.A: Criteria defined in advance are anchored to the task's requirements, not shaped by what was actually produced.
options.B: Post-hoc criteria are prohibited by standard quality-management frameworks.
options.C: Defining criteria afterward risks triggering unnecessary regeneration cycles.
options.D: Pre-defined criteria allow the model to self-evaluate during generation and correct before finishing.

items.question: Which TWO properties characterize a well-calibrated output? (Choose TWO)

options.A: The output contains no arithmetic computation errors.
options.B: Confidence expressed in claims corresponds to the actual likelihood those claims are correct.
options.C: All assertions trace back to documents present in the context window.
options.D: Uncertainty is explicitly acknowledged when a claim is genuinely difficult to verify.
options.E: Output length is proportional to the complexity of the task.
